newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia says would crush separatists if war flared.
newsitem.headline: Georgia says would crush separatists if war flared.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze warned separatists in the breakaway region of Abkhazia on Wednesday that they would be committing "suicide" if they chose to go to war again with a rebuilt Georgian army.

"The armed forces of Georgia are not the same as we had in 1992-93. If the Abkhaz open fire, then that means suicide for them," Shevardnadze told a news conference in the capital, Tbilisi. He was referring to the Abkhaz victory in 1992-93.
The warning from the former Soviet foreign minister came a day after he offered a new start to peace negotiations, while ruling out any solution that recognised Abkhazian independence.
Shevardnadze was forced to flee the region under fire when his troops were routed in 1993 by pro-independence Abkhaz-led fighters after a year of fighting in which an estimated 10,000 people died.
The debacle, and a subsequent civil war in Georgia, wrecked the former Soviet republic's armed forces.
Abkhazia, a subtropical region on the Black Sea once favoured by Moscow's communist elite as a beach resort, has run itself as a de facto independent state since the conflict.

But no country has recognised its sovereignty and a partial blockade imposed by Russia and other former Soviet republics in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) has plunged Abkhazia into deep isolation and ruined its once-rich economy.
Fears have risen in Georgia recently about the possibility of new conflict with Abkhazia if 2,500 Russian peacekeepers now patrolling the confrontation line are withdrawn.

Georgia insists the peacekeepers, who have been there since 1994, must go home after their present mandate expires on July 31 unless they agree to take on increased duties that include a wider zone of operations and helping to repatriate refugees.
Observers say the departure of the Russian peacekeepers could leave a dangerous vacuum which could reignite the war.
Shevardnadze, stressing the peacekeeping mandate's deadline, urged the Abkhaz to agree to new negotiations to reopen a peace process which has reached a dead end.
"The peacekeeping forces will stay in Abkhazia until the end of July. During these two months, we have all the basis for a direct dialogue," he said.
The CIS has approved the wider role for the peacekeepers but the Russians say they are opposed to taking them up unless the Abkhaz drop their vociferous objections.
Shevardnadze said that, even if the Russians left, Georgia would not start a military campaign to retake the province.
"War for us is unacceptable. For the Abkhaz it means suicide and the destruction of their nation.
